question: Which muscle tissue type is under voluntary control?
explanation: Skeletal muscles attach to bones and allow conscious, voluntary control over body movements. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h1)

question: What special feature helps cardiac muscle cells connect and pass electrical signals quickly?
explanation: Think of intercalated discs as special communication highways between heart cells. They let electrical impulses zip right through so your heart beats as one smooth team! [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h1)

question: Which two main proteins make up the tiny filaments inside a muscle sarcomere?
explanation: Actin (the thin one) and myosin (the thick one) are the dynamic duo inside your muscles that slide together to create movement. Brilliant! [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h2)

question: What is the chemical neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction?
explanation: Acetylcholine is released from motor neurons to cross the synapse and stimulate muscle fiber membranes. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h3)

question: A patient is given a drug that blocks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. What happens as a result?
explanation: If the chemical messenger can't deliver its message because the receptors are blocked, the muscle simply cannot receive the signal to contract. That leads to relaxation and paralysis! [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h3)

question: Which part of a resting muscle cell acts as a storage house for calcium ions?
explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is like a tiny calcium bank inside the muscle cell, holding onto calcium until it's time for action! [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h4)

question: What is the main job of T-tubules during muscle contraction?

options.A: They produce the ATP required for cross-bridge cycling
options.B: They store calcium ions until a contraction begins
options.C: They carry the electrical action potential deep into the muscle fiber
options.D: They anchor thin actin filaments to the Z-lines

explanation: Think of T-tubules as underground tunnels that carry surface electrical signals straight to the deep core of the muscle cell so everything contracts together. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h4)

question: What happens to the actual length of thick and thin filaments when a muscle contracts?

options.A: They stretch out to make the sarcomere longer
options.B: They shorten significantly as the muscle contracts
options.C: They dissolve completely and reform later
options.D: They stay the same length while sliding past each other

explanation: A common trick question! The filaments themselves don't shrink or stretch; they just slide past each other like two combs interlocking. Smooth moves! [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h5)

question: Why must calcium bind to troponin before a muscle can contract?

options.A: It directly provides the energy needed for the power stroke
options.B: It moves tropomyosin away from actin binding sites
options.C: It holds the Z-lines firmly in place during movement
options.D: It destroys excess acetylcholine in the synapse

explanation: At rest, tropomyosin blocks the binding sites like a locked door. Calcium acts as the key that shifts it out of the way so the muscle can get to work! [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h5)

question: What is the main job of ATP when it binds to myosin during muscle contraction?

options.A: To allow the myosin head to detach from actin
options.B: To release acetylcholine into the synapse
options.C: To pull the Z-lines further apart
options.D: To instantly activate the sarcoplasmic reticulum

explanation: ATP is the energy currency that acts like a release button, letting the myosin head disconnect from actin so it can reset for the next pull. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h6)

question: What causes the stiffness of rigor mortis after a person passes away?

options.A: An excessive buildup of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction
options.B: Continuous nerve signals firing from the brain
options.C: A lack of ATP preventing myosin heads from detaching from actin
options.D: The permanent destruction of troponin within the sarcomere

explanation: Without cellular energy (ATP) to act as the release button, muscles can't let go. They stay locked in place, causing that classic post-mortem stiffness. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h6)

question: Which enzyme breaks down acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction so the muscle can finally relax?
explanation: Acetylcholinesterase is the clean-up crew enzyme that sweeps away leftover acetylcholine so the muscle doesn't stay stuck in a constant contraction. Well done! [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h7)

question: What direct action allows a muscle fiber to return to its normal resting length?

options.A: Fresh ATP binds directly to the actin filaments
options.B: Motor neurons release more potassium into the sarcoplasm
options.C: Calcium ions are pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
options.D: Tropomyosin permanently detaches from the Z-lines

explanation: When the calcium is safely sucked back into storage, the blocking proteins snap back into place, letting the muscle rest and relax. You're crushing this! [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h7)
